course: an illustrated online course on how large computer systems are designed
intro: Each lesson opens on a real system, outage or published paper (LiveJournal's cache, Google's file system, Amazon's Dynamo, Spanner's clocks), puts the reader in front of the problem its builders met, then shows the design they published, in the plain, concrete voice of the site's other courses. Numbers over adjectives: latencies in milliseconds, rates a second, costs in machines. Keep technical terms exact (replica, quorum, idempotent, percentile, consensus, lease); don't soften them. No buzzwords used as explanations.
voice:
Write straightforward, conventional technical documentation. Strip out any faux-profound or aphoristic tone. Replace dramatic colons, omitted verbs (gapping) and overly simplified phrasing (such as "where the time goes") with standard, explicit engineering terminology. Always include units of measurement. Make the reader or the engineer the subject of a sentence, not the "lesson" or the "steps". In particular, as guidance (exceptions are fine where they read better):
1. Use precise technical terms (latency, queueing, bottleneck, throughput) rather than vague plain-English substitutes ("where the time goes", "requests waiting for each other").
2. No dramatic colons that deliver a punchline, maxim or takeaway at the end of a sentence.
3. No inanimate agency: write "In this lesson, we will design..." rather than "This lesson designs...".
4. No verb ellipsis and no dropped units: write "210 ms", not "210", and keep the verbs in compound clauses.
5. No theatrical mentoring ("say it out loud", "paid three times over"); explain concepts plainly.
